text: {"user":"I’m planning a house refresh: I want to repaint the living room this weekend, but I’m also deciding what to do about the old smoke stains on the ceiling. I have a roller and extension pole already; I can either buy a dedicated stain-blocking primer or just use the regular primer I have on hand and do a second coat later. Which approach should I follow, and are there any prep steps I shouldn’t skip?","plus_response":"For smoke stains, I’d strongly favor the stain-blocking primer (the cheaper regular primer “I have on hand” often turns into repeated coats). In practice, a stain-blocking product is usually the lower total cost because it prevents bleed-through, so you don’t end up re-priming and repainting multiple times. Prep-wise, scrape any loose paint, wash the area to remove residue, let it dry fully, then apply the primer specifically over the stained spots (feather the edges). After that, repaint with your chosen finish; if you do the prep well, you should be able to keep it to the planned number of coats instead of escalating later.","minus_response":"I’d go with the regular primer you already have if you’re planning to repaint anyway—then use an extra coat only where needed after the first layer dries. For smoke stains, the key is thorough prep: clean the ceiling so the primer can adhere, address any flaking or loose paint by scraping and sanding smooth, and make sure everything is completely dry before priming. After priming, apply your topcoat and assess coverage under good light; a second coat in just the stained areas is often enough. This approach keeps the process straightforward while still achieving a uniform final look."}
